name: Screen curfew / dopamine detox

card.summary: Cutting screens before bed and taking breaks from stimulation; the light-and-sleep logic has support, the "dopamine" framing is disputed.

quick.overview:
A screen curfew stops device use before bed. Dopamine detox goes further and abstains from stimulating activities for a period.

Evening-light research gives the first a basis for sleep; the second has no defined protocol or trials.
quick.mechanism: Device light can delay the body clock and melatonin. Dopamine fasting is said to reduce impulsive habits rather than dopamine itself.
quick.risks: No direct harms are documented, though extreme versions of dopamine fasting have been criticized by clinicians.

lead: A screen curfew means stopping phone, computer and TV use some time before bed, and "dopamine detox" or "dopamine fasting" is a related practice of temporarily abstaining from stimulating activities such as scrolling, gaming and snacking. In looksmaxxing and self-improvement communities both are used to get better sleep and focus, and to free time for training, skincare and other habits that change how a person looks.

The appearance chain runs through sleep. Evening light from phones, tablets and LEDs can delay circadian timing and reduce sleep quality.[1] In an experimental BMJ study, people photographed after sleep restriction were rated less healthy and less attractive than after a normal night, and later work measured changes in skin colour, eye openness, mouth curvature and periorbital darkness after sleep deprivation.[4][5][6]

Dopamine fasting was popularised by California psychologist Cameron Sepah, who says it is a cognitive behavioural technique targeting impulsive behaviours rather than a literal lowering of dopamine; neuroscientists have criticised the name and the idea of a brain "reset".[2] Wikipedia's articles on sleep hygiene and digital detoxes describe the wider practice of managing evening light and device time.[3][11]

chain: Screens are switched off before bed and impulsive habits are reduced
Easier sleep onset and more time for training and routines
Rested, healthier-looking face and more consistent self-care
angle.text: People use a curfew and breaks from stimulation to sleep better and spend less time scrolling. The looks payoff they describe is a fresher appearance and more time for gym and grooming habits.

infobox: No phone before bed; breaks from social media, gaming, snacking
Melanopsin-containing retinal cells, most sensitive near 480 nm blue light [1]

paras: A screen curfew sets a cut-off time in the evening after which phones, tablets, computers and televisions are put away. Some people also keep the phone out of the bedroom, switch on night modes or greyscale, or avoid screens in the first hour after waking. Dopamine detox or fasting is broader and less defined: a set period, from a day to a few weeks, of staying away from scrolling, short-form video, gaming, snacks, music or other highly rewarding activities, replaced with exercise, reading, outdoors time or sleep [2][7].

Both practices are used in appearance-focused communities as no-cost habits. The reasoning offered runs through sleep and consistency: a person who sleeps more regularly and spends less evening time on a screen has more energy and time for training, skincare and grooming, and may look more rested [4][5][6][7].

The practice rests on research on evening light. A small group of intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells containing the photopigment melanopsin sends light signals to the brain's circadian pacemaker in the suprachiasmatic nucleus; melanopsin is most sensitive to blue light near 480 nanometres, and light in this range suppresses melatonin, raises alertness and shifts circadian timing [1].

Wikipedia's article on light and circadian rhythm notes that these cells may respond to light as dim as about 1 lux, far below the 2,500 lux once thought necessary to suppress melatonin, and states that blue light from phones, tablets and LEDs can delay sleep onset and reduce sleep quality [1]. It cites experiments showing that lower-intensity short-wavelength light advanced human circadian rhythms about as well as brighter white light (Warman et al., 2003) and that 460 nm light reduced sleepiness and raised heart rate during a 1.5-hour exposure (Cajochen et al., 2005) [1]. It also lists a 2015 PNAS study of evening light-emitting e-readers, which examined effects on sleep, circadian timing and next-morning alertness [1].

General sleep-hygiene advice recommends bright natural light during the day and avoiding bright light in the hours before bed, along with regular sleep times, a dark, quiet, cool bedroom, and avoiding caffeine and other stimulants late in the day [3]. Wikipedia's sleep hygiene article reports that evidence is strongest for noise, alcohol before sleep, mentally demanding tasks before bed and trying too hard to fall asleep, and that sleep hygiene alone is inconclusively effective for insomnia while showing better results alongside cognitive behavioural therapy [3].

A 2021 American Academy of Sleep Medicine meta-analysis did not favour sleep hygiene as a stand-alone treatment for chronic insomnia, and could not evaluate individual items because study methods differed; a 2014 review had likewise called the evidence weak and inconclusive [3]. The term traces back to Willard Moyer's 1903 phrase "hygiene of sleep" and entered modern sleep medicine through Peter Hauri's 1977 book No More Sleepless Nights [3].

The connection to looks comes from studies of sleep loss. In the 2010 BMJ experiment on "beauty sleep", observers rated photographs of people after restricted sleep as less healthy and less attractive than photographs taken after normal sleep [4]. A 2017 study reported that restricted sleep changed facial appearance and social appeal, and a 2019 study measured objective and subjective facial changes after sleep deprivation, such as skin colour, eye openness, mouth curvature and periorbital darkness [5][6]. Wikipedia's sleep deprivation article lists periorbital puffiness, or eye bags, among its effects [12].
These studies tested sleep restriction, not screen curfews, so any link from a curfew to a fresher appearance runs through whether the curfew changes how long and how well a person sleeps.

Dopamine fasting was developed by California psychologist Cameron Sepah as a cognitive behavioural technique for impulsive and behavioural addictions, and he coined the name, which he later called misleading [2]. It has no fixed definition: some versions restrict only online technology, others also work, exercise, physical contact and unnecessary conversation, and the most extreme imaginable form is complete sensory deprivation [2]. Targets include social media, gaming, shopping, emotional eating, gambling and pornography [2].

Sepah has said the goal is to reduce impulsive behaviour, not dopamine itself [2]. Neuroscientist Ciara McCabe describes the practice as avoiding cues, such as a phone's ringtone, that trigger compulsive follow-up behaviour [2]. Proponents describe it as a reaction to products designed to hold attention and as a way to make room for reading, crafts or outdoor sport, and say it builds self-discipline; New York Times technology reporter Nellie Bowles described a practitioner whose life became more exciting and fun [2].

Coverage peaked in late 2019 and early 2020: Katie Way in Vice on 17 October 2019, Nellie Bowles in The New York Times on 7 November, John Grohol at Psych Central, Julie Fraga at Mic and Maria Coole in Marie Claire [2]. Physician Peter Grinspoon called Sepah's underlying approach sensible if not groundbreaking, but described followers' ever more ascetic versions as unhealthy, and in a February 2020 Harvard Health blog called the trend a maladaptive fad built on misunderstood science [2].

Critics, including McCabe, say the idea that the brain can be reset by avoiding dopamine triggers is scientifically unfounded, and that removing a stimulus lowers stimulation rather than dopamine, which plays vital roles in everyday functioning [2]. Christopher Ferguson (2018) argued that technology use has never been conclusively shown to desensitise the brain to dopamine [2]. Wikipedia also cites a 2024 genetically informed study of adults aged 30 to 45 finding more screen time linked to higher impulsivity, and notes that replacing poor habits with exercise is associated with increased grey matter in reward-related regions [2].

A digital detox is a deliberate break from devices that can range from limits on use to complete abstinence, usually for a week to a month. Moderate approaches include set times for social media, screen-free mornings and evenings and fewer notifications [11]. Wikipedia summarises mixed findings: detoxes have been linked to less eye strain and neck pain, a 2023 meta-analysis found small well-being gains from less social media use, a 2024 meta-analysis found reduced depression but no significant effect on well-being or stress, and a month-long randomised trial in PNAS Nexus in February 2025 found that restricting mobile internet access improved mental health, well-being and sustained attention [11].

On looksmax.org, threads promote dopamine detoxes as a way to escape constant stimulation from scrolling, rapid content and notifications and to become more productive. One widely read thread proposes a seven-day plan with limits on social media, no phone in the bedroom, no screen for the first hour of the morning and replacement with lifting, reading and sunlight [7]. Other users report mixed results; one thread describes cutting social media, music and most device time for a week, using a greyscale phone, and still finding everything bland, while a reply calls dopamine detox and abstinence a form of 'cope' [8]. Hacker News posted several videos on the topic in 2023 [9][10]. A companion page covers abstaining from pornography and masturbation as part of detoxes.

No studies found of dopamine fasting or a formal screen curfew as defined in these communities. Related research covers evening light exposure and sleep [1], sleep hygiene as a general category with inconclusive results [3], digital detoxes as a broader category with mixed results [11], and how restricted sleep changes facial appearance [4][5][6].

No direct harms from a screen curfew are documented. Clinicians have cautioned about extreme dopamine-fasting versions that restrict food, conversation or all stimulation, and Grinspoon reported in a 2024 Inc. article that most dopamine detoxes do more harm than good in his view [2]. Digital detoxes can also increase social pressure and fear of missing out for some people [11].

Peter Hauri's No More Sleepless Nights brings sleep hygiene into modern sleep medicine [3].

lore.intro: Dopamine detox appears on looksmax.org as a discipline and productivity practice, with accounts both enthusiastic and underwhelmed.[7][8]

claims.claim: Constant scrolling overstimulates the brain, and a detox resets focus.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread opens by saying most people's brains are constantly overstimulated by scrolling, rapid content and notifications, and promotes a detox for focus and productivity.[7]
claims.experts: Neuroscientist Ciara McCabe has called the idea of resetting the brain through short abstinence nonsense, and Sepah says the practice targets impulsive behaviour rather than dopamine.[2]

claims.claim: A week of cutting out stimulation transforms how you feel.
claims.believers: Some users attempt full abstinence from social media, music and extra device use, with a greyscale phone; one reports everything still felt bland afterward.[8]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes it has not been conclusively shown that technology use desensitises the brain to dopamine.[2]

claims.believers: Curfew advocates say evening phone use keeps them awake and makes them look tired.
claims.experts: Reference sources describe evening light, especially blue-rich light, as able to delay circadian timing and reduce sleep quality.[1]

claims.claim: Better sleep from a curfew makes you look better.
claims.believers: Practitioners say a regular sleep schedule leaves them looking fresher and with more energy for training and grooming.
claims.experts: Experimental studies found that people photographed after restricted sleep were rated less healthy and less attractive.[4][5][6] None tested a screen curfew.

claims.claim: Light blocking and night modes are enough on their own.
claims.believers: Some posters rely on greyscale phones or filters rather than stopping device use.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that sleep hygiene measures alone are inconclusive for insomnia, and a 2021 AASM meta-analysis did not favour them as a stand-alone treatment.[3]

claims.claim: Digital detoxes improve mood and attention.
claims.believers: Forum guides present reduced social media as a route to clarity and productivity.[7]
claims.experts: Meta-analyses of detoxes report small or mixed effects, while a 2025 randomised trial of restricting mobile internet found improved mental health and attention.[11]
